newsitem.title: CANADA: GM Canada-union talks face Wednesday deadline.
newsitem.headline: GM Canada-union talks face Wednesday deadline.

text.p: With little more than three days before a strike deadline, General Motors Corp. and the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union remained at odds over work by outside contractors and other issues, union officials said.

The union chose G.M. Canada on Monday as its second negotiating target after reaching agreement with Chrysler Canada earlier this month. The Chrysler pact, ratified last weekend, halts plant sales and closings during the three-year agreement and commits Chrysler to replace any union jobs lost due to work done by outside contractors, known as outsourcing.

But GM, the world's largest automaker, has shown little interest in accepting the terms the union bargained with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian subisidiary. The union has set a strike deadline of 11:59 P.M. EDT on Wednesday (3:59 A.M. GMT Thursday morning).
Talks continued at a Toronto hotel on Sunday and the union planned to hold a news conference on Monday to discuss the status of negotiations, a union official said.

G.M. Canada president Maureen Kempston-Darkes wrote in a letter to her employees last week that the other North American and Japanese automakers in Canada had an advantage over G.M. because they contracted out more production.

"GM now needs to take the steps already set in place by Ford (Motor Co.) and Chrysler to become more competitive -- we need to go further to become as productive and competitive as the Japanese transplants here in Canada and the U.S."
At the heart of the disagreement is the CAW's determination to restrict outsourcing and reverse G.M. Canada's intentions to sell two plants and contract out about 5,500 union jobs.

CAW President Buzz Hargrove told reporters on Friday that he had agreed to G.M.'s insistence that he meet with a secret prospective buyer for the automaker's Oshawa and Windsor, Ontario, parts plants.
"I told him you can buy if you want, you buy us, but you also buy the CAW-GM master collective agreement," he said.
Hargove said the union has approved an escalating strike strategy that would close a few G.M. plants at a time until all of its operations were shut down.
"Our union has unanimously approved a selective and escalating strike strategy," he said.

If no agreement is reached by the deadline, Hargrove said the union will shut down G.M. operations in Oshawa and St. Therese, Quebec. He said members will walk out of G.M.'s St. Catharines plant on October 6 and close down remaining plants in London and Windsor, also in Ontario, on October 9.
Analysts said a strike could cost General Motors as much as $150 million a week, halt production of some vehicle models and interrupt U.S. operations.

"A long strike might get to the point where it would be reducing G.M.'s profits by maybe $100 million to $150 million a week," said Dave Healy, analyst at Burnham Securities Inc. "It could spread south of the (Canada/U.S.) border as well."

But he said a Canadian strike would not reach the same proportions as an earlier strike at G.M. this year when United Auto Workers union members at a Dayton, Ohio, brake plant walked off the job over outsourcing. The strike lasted 17 days, shut virtually all GM's North American operations and cost the carmaker $900 million over 17 days.

The CAW's $36.7 million strike fund may make it tough to carry out a long-term strike and pay strike benefits to 28,000 members at GM. But Hargrove said last week that the union had called a special strike dues convention for the entire 210,000-member union on October 18 as a contingency.

The union leader said that if no agreement is reached, it would be the first time that a company had failed to accept a so-called pattern agreement. Traditionally the union sets the pattern with one company and applies that agreement to other automakers.
